title: For the sick and afraid
hookLine: the sound of a waiting room; Shantideva's list of wishes starts far away and comes close to home
tomorrow: what does an old poem wish someone stuck at the airport?

lines: THEN IT COMES CLOSE TO HOME.
cards: Waiting rooms have their own sound. A TV nobody is watching. The hum of a vending machine.
Somebody's knee bouncing, a phone buzzing, a name called that isn't yours. Shantideva's list of wishes passes through rooms like that, but it doesn't start there.
It starts far off, in the hells of Buddhist teaching: may the cold find warmth, may the burning be cooled. Then the animals.
Then, verse by verse, it comes closer, to the blind, the hungry, and then right into the waiting room: the sick, and the afraid.

teach.b: Here's the wish, in plain words. May the sick be freed from sickness.

May the frightened stop being afraid. May the ones who are tied up go free, and the ones with no strength find some. And then the line closes on something quieter: may people think of helping one another.
Notice what Shantideva can't do. A verse doesn't set a bone or shrink a fever, and the poem doesn't claim it does. So what's the wish for?
Go back to chapter one of his guide.

teach.h: FIRST THE WISH, THEN THE ROAD.
teach.b: There he says there's wishing to go and actually going, like deciding on a trip and then walking the road. The wish comes first. It's how the bodhisattva's way begins.
A wish said for a sick friend doesn't replace the casserole or the ride to the appointment. It's the thing that gets you to bring them. And the last line shows where the whole list has been heading.
It isn't only that the sick get well.
It's that people start looking out for each other.
Say it slowly and listen to it: may they be well. Four words, and nobody is left out of they.

how: Wishing well-being for others is part of daily practice in Buddhist communities; Mahayana practitioners recite dedication verses like Shantideva's, and loving-kindness wishes are said for the sick and the frightened by name.

games.q: what does “for the sick and afraid” mean?
o: a promise that a verse will make sick people well
a warning to stay away from anyone who is ill
wishing healing and an end to fear for others

games.q: the wishes, one by one — tap the pairs.

s: Shantideva's list of wishes begins with the sick
it begins far off, in the hells of Buddhist teaching, then comes close to home.
the wish ends by hoping people will help one another
the list heads somewhere: not only healing, but people looking out for each other.
a wish you can't act on right away is pointless
chapter one says the wish to go comes first, and leads to the going.

games.q: your grandpa is in the hospital three states away, and you can't visit until next month. what fits Shantideva's verses?
o: wish him well every day, and let the wish turn into calls and cards.
nothing until you can be there; a wish from far away is only words.
try not to think about it, since worrying won't heal him anyway.
games.why: the verses don't claim to heal anyone. the wish comes first, like deciding on a trip, and it's what gets you on the road: the call, the card.

practice: Rest one hand open. For each of three people, press a fingertip to your thumb: someone who is sick, someone who is afraid, and someone you don't know at all. With each small press, say under your breath: may they be well.
Then let the hand open and rest.

wordCard.voice: For the sick and afraid: Shantideva's verses wishing healing to the sick and an end to fear for the frightened.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: fearlessness, freedom from fear. What the verse wishes for the frightened.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: may they be well, said even on the days you can't fix a thing. That's forty-seven.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 10.2–10.20 (wishes for beings in the hells, animals, the blind, the hungry; may the sick be freed, the frightened be fearless, the bound be freed, the weak gain strength, and people think of one another's good)
Bodhicaryavatara 1.15–1.16 (wishing to go and going: aspiring and engaged bodhicitta)
